overview.prompt: A client with newly diagnosed triple-negative breast cancer says, “That means nothing can be done for me.” What is the nurse’s best response?

options.text: “That’s right; no treatment works for this type of cancer.”
“It describes the tumor’s receptors; treatments still exist.”
“It means the cancer has spread to several lymph nodes.”
“It means you carry several inherited BRCA variants.”

overview.rationale: Triple-negative means ER-negative, PR-negative, and HER2-negative; it does not mean no treatments exist. It does not describe node count or inherited variants.

overview.prompt: A client with an abnormal Pap result asks what usually leads to cervical cancer. Which response is accurate?

options.text: Frequent long-term tampon use
Persistent high-risk HPV infection
A single episode of yeast infection
Long-term unopposed estrogen

overview.rationale: Cervical cancer usually begins in the transformation zone after persistent high-risk HPV infection. Unopposed estrogen is an endometrial cancer risk.

overview.prompt: A postmenopausal client with a uterus has taken estrogen-only therapy for years. Which cancer risk does this most directly raise?

options.text: Endometrial cancer
HPV-related cancer
Ovarian cancer
Cervical cancer

overview.rationale: Unopposed estrogen, obesity/chronic anovulation, estrogen-only therapy in a person with a uterus, and tamoxifen are relevant endometrial cancer risks. Cervical and other HPV-related cancers are driven by persistent high-risk HPV, not unopposed estrogen.

overview.prompt: A client’s breast cancer is HER2-positive, and she asks if her daughters should be tested for it. What is the nurse’s best response?

options.text: “Yes, HER2 is passed directly from mother to child.”
“HER2 is a tumor marker, not an inherited-risk test.”
“HER2 results show the cancer risk in your family.”
“HER2 testing is the same as BRCA blood testing.”

overview.rationale: Tumor HER2 testing is different from inherited-risk testing; HER2 is chiefly a tumor biomarker, while germline BRCA testing informs family risk.

manifestations.prompt: A client asks about breast changes. Which statements by the nurse are accurate? Select all that apply.

options.text: A painful lump does not need to be checked
Tender armpit nodes rule out a cancer cause
A soft, mobile lump can still need evaluation
Skin dimpling is an expected change with age
Many cancers show on imaging before a lump

manifestations.rationale: A soft, mobile, or painful finding can still need evaluation, and many cancers are detected on imaging before a lump is felt. Tenderness or its absence is not an independent cancer test, and skin dimpling/retraction is a warning finding that warrants evaluation.

manifestations.prompt: A client was treated with antibiotics for presumed mastitis, but the breast remains rapidly and diffusely red and swollen. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Reassure her that this redness is from the infection
Arrange prompt evaluation for inflammatory cancer
Continue the same antibiotic for another full month
Apply warm packs and recheck at her yearly mammogram

manifestations.rationale: Rapid diffuse redness/swelling may indicate inflammatory breast cancer and warrants prompt assessment, including when initially thought to be infection. Prolonging antibiotics or waiting for routine screening delays diagnosis.

manifestations.prompt: A 58-year-old client reports 4 weeks of new daily bloating, feeling full quickly, and pelvic discomfort. What should the nurse recognize?

options.text: These persistent symptoms need ovarian/tubal evaluation
These symptoms matter just if a mass is felt
These are normal effects of aging and need no workup
These are explained by a recent large meal

manifestations.rationale: Persistent/new bloating, early satiety, and pelvic/abdominal discomfort should prompt evaluation; persistence and change from baseline matter.

manifestations.prompt: A 62-year-old client, menopausal for 10 years, reports light vaginal spotting. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Reassure her that spotting is normal after menopause
Arrange diagnostic evaluation of the bleeding
Wait for her next routine screening Pap test
Suggest a vaginal moisturizer and no follow-up

manifestations.rationale: Abnormal uterine bleeding, especially any bleeding after menopause, is the hallmark of endometrial cancer and needs diagnostic evaluation, not just a screening Pap test. Reassurance or waiting delays diagnosis.

risk.prompt: Which factors increase breast cancer risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Regular moderate activity
An inherited pathogenic BRCA1 or BRCA2 variant
Dense breast tissue on scans
Increasing age in women
Prior high-dose chest radiation

risk.rationale: Increasing age, an inherited pathogenic BRCA1/BRCA2 variant, dense breast tissue, and prior high-dose chest radiation increase breast cancer risk. A benign variant or variant of uncertain significance is not equivalent to a pathogenic finding. Regular moderate activity is protective rather than a risk factor.

risk.prompt: A postmenopausal client asks which lifestyle changes may lower her breast cancer risk. Which factors should the nurse address?

options.text: Caffeine, dairy, and underwire bras
Low-fat yogurt, fish, and whole grains
Antiperspirants, hair dye, and cold weather
Alcohol, inactivity, and excess body weight

risk.rationale: Alcohol, physical inactivity, and excess body weight particularly after menopause contribute to breast cancer risk. The other items are not listed as risk factors.

risk.prompt: A premenopausal client at increased risk asks about risk-reducing medicine. Which agent may be used in both pre- and postmenopausal clients?

options.text: Raloxifene
Tamoxifen
Letrozole
Anastrozole

risk.rationale: Tamoxifen can be used in pre/postmenopausal patients; raloxifene or an aromatase inhibitor (such as anastrozole or letrozole) is for selected postmenopausal patients.

diagnostics.prompt: A client’s mammogram and ultrasound show a suspicious mass. She asks if she has cancer. What establishes the diagnosis?

options.text: The mammogram report alone
Tissue pathology from biopsy
A tumor-marker blood test
A breast MRI result alone

diagnostics.rationale: Tissue pathology establishes the diagnosis and reports type and grade; imaging alone does not provide a tissue diagnosis.

diagnostics.prompt: A client scheduled for sentinel lymph node biopsy asks its purpose. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: It samples the first draining nodes for staging
It confirms the tumor’s hormone receptor status
It treats the cancer by removing the whole tumor
It removes the whole chain of armpit nodes

diagnostics.rationale: SLNB samples the first draining node(s) for staging, usually with less morbidity than full axillary dissection. It is not full dissection, receptor testing, or tumor removal.

diagnostics.prompt: A client is scheduled for a mammogram this afternoon. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: Drink an oral contrast solution before arriving
Fast from midnight until the mammogram is done
Follow guidance about deodorant or powder that day
Hold your usual medications for the week before

diagnostics.rationale: Follow instructions about deodorant/lotion/powder on the breast/axilla that day, and explain brief compression. Fasting, contrast, and holding usual medicines are not required.

diagnostics.prompt: After an endometrial biopsy, which client report should be reported promptly?

options.text: Feeling tired that evening
Light spotting for a few days
Soaking a pad within an hour
Mild cramping that eases off

diagnostics.rationale: Report heavy bleeding (for example, soaking a pad in an hour), severe pain, fever, or foul discharge; mild cramps/spotting can last a few days.

medical.prompt: A client will receive chemotherapy before her lumpectomy. How should the nurse describe this approach?

options.text: Palliative therapy, given for symptom relief
Neoadjuvant therapy, given before surgery
Adjuvant therapy, given after surgery
Maintenance therapy, given after remission

medical.rationale: Neoadjuvant therapy is given before surgery, and adjuvant therapy is given after surgery. Palliative and maintenance therapy describe different goals and timing.

medical.prompt: A premenopausal client asks if her mastectomy will put her into menopause. Which response is accurate?

options.text: “Menopause begins once the drains are removed.”
“Lumpectomy, not mastectomy, causes menopause.”
“Yes, mastectomy causes immediate menopause.”
“Breast surgery alone doesn’t cause menopause.”

medical.rationale: Breast surgery alone does not cause surgical menopause; ovarian removal or ovarian-suppressing/gonadotoxic treatment can.

medical.prompt: A client is diagnosed with endometrial cancer. Which treatment does the nurse anticipate is most common?

options.text: Hysterectomy with BSO and staging
Watchful observation without surgery
A breast cancer endocrine regimen
Tamoxifen as the primary treatment

medical.rationale: Endometrial cancer is commonly treated with hysterectomy with bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy and surgical staging; breast regimens are not copied to pelvic cancers.

medications.prompt: A client is receiving doxorubicin. Which agent-specific concern should the nurse monitor?

options.text: Peripheral neuropathy as the main dose-limiting toxicity
Cumulative cardiac injury and vesicant extravasation
Retinal toxicity that requires regular eye exams
Hemorrhagic cystitis as the main dose-limiting toxicity

medications.rationale: Doxorubicin carries cumulative cardiac injury and vesicant extravasation risks. Bladder injury is linked to cyclophosphamide and neuropathy to paclitaxel.

medications.prompt: A client taking tamoxifen reports new abnormal vaginal bleeding. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Wait for the next routine Pap test
Advise stopping tamoxifen independently
Reassure that this is expected
Ensure prompt diagnostic evaluation

medications.rationale: Tamoxifen carries uterine/endometrial risk, so abnormal vaginal bleeding should be reported and investigated. Stopping independently or waiting is inappropriate.

medications.prompt: A client is starting trastuzumab (Herceptin). Which monitoring should the nurse ensure is arranged?

options.text: Daily fingerstick glucose checks
Weekly audiometry hearing tests
Baseline and interval LVEF checks
Monthly bone density (DXA) scans

medications.rationale: Assess baseline and interval LVEF/cardiac function and heart-failure symptoms, because HER2 therapy can cause cardiac dysfunction. The other tests are not trastuzumab monitoring.

medications.prompt: A premenopausal client with HR-positive breast cancer is prescribed letrozole. What does the nurse expect to accompany it?

options.text: Added trastuzumab infusions
Ovarian suppression therapy
A daily estrogen supplement
Letrozole alone as monotherapy

medications.rationale: In premenopausal patients, aromatase inhibitors require ovarian suppression rather than use as effective monotherapy. Estrogen would counteract treatment.

nonpharmacological.prompt: A client hears conflicting advice about mammogram screening schedules. Which response is accurate?

options.text: “The major groups agree on a yearly schedule.”
“Screening begins once a lump can be felt.”
“More frequent screening is better for everyone.”
“Schedules differ, so the source should be named.”

nonpharmacological.rationale: Average-risk schedules differ: USPSTF recommends mammography every 2 years from ages 40–74, while ACR/SBI recommends annual screening from 40, so the source should be labeled. Symptomatic assessment is different from routine screening, and more frequent imaging is not automatically better.

nonpharmacological.prompt: Under the final 2018 USPSTF recommendation, which asymptomatic, average-risk client with a cervix is below the recommended age to begin routine cervical screening?

options.text: A 19-year-old client
A 35-year-old client
A 25-year-old client
A 55-year-old client

nonpharmacological.rationale: USPSTF (2018 final) recommends no screening under 21; ages 21–29 have Pap/cytology every 3 years, and ages 30–65 have Pap, primary hrHPV, or cotesting options. ACS uses a different starting age (25), so the guideline should be labeled.

nonpharmacological.prompt: A young adult client completed the HPV vaccine series and asks if she still needs cervical screening. What is the nurse’s best response?

options.text: “No, the vaccine takes the place of screening.”
“Yes, screening remains recommended after it.”
“Just if you develop symptoms such as bleeding.”
“Not until you are much older than you are now.”

nonpharmacological.rationale: HPV vaccination does not remove screening needs; symptoms or abnormal results need diagnostic follow-up.

adverse-effects.prompt: A client receiving chemotherapy calls with a temperature of 100.4°F (38°C) but feels otherwise fine. What should the nurse advise?

options.text: Take acetaminophen and recheck tomorrow
Wait for chills before calling back
Call oncology now for urgent assessment
Wait to see if the fever rises further

adverse-effects.rationale: A temperature ≥100.4°F (38°C) during chemotherapy warrants an immediate oncology call/urgent assessment; do not wait or mask the fever.

adverse-effects.prompt: A client after sentinel lymph node biopsy asks if she can still get lymphedema. Which response is accurate?

options.text: “Lymphedema follows radiation, not SLNB.”
“Lymphedema stops being a risk after a year.”
“Lymphedema happens just after full dissection.”
“SLNB lowers the risk but doesn’t remove it.”

adverse-effects.rationale: Sentinel biopsy reduces but does not eliminate lymphedema risk, so new swelling or tightness should be reported. Lymphedema is not limited to radiation or to the first year.

adverse-effects.prompt: A client taking anastrozole reports joint aches. Which adverse effects are associated with aromatase inhibitors?

options.text: Hemorrhagic cystitis and hair loss
Cardiac dysfunction and infusion reactions
Hot flashes with uterine cancer risk
Arthralgia, bone loss, and fractures

adverse-effects.rationale: AIs cause arthralgia, bone loss, and fractures. Uterine risk is linked to tamoxifen and cardiac dysfunction to HER2 therapy.

nutrition.prompt: A client with chemotherapy-related mouth sores asks what to eat. Which choice is best?

options.text: Crunchy toast and crackers
Citrus juice for vitamin C
Spicy foods to boost appetite
Soft, bland, moist foods

nutrition.rationale: For mucositis, choose soft, bland, moist foods; avoid very hot, rough/crunchy, acidic, or irritating foods.

nutrition.prompt: A client with significant immunosuppression asks about food safety. Which guidance is appropriate?

options.text: Avoid raw fruits and vegetables throughout treatment
Eat canned or packaged foods until treatment ends
Fresh unpasteurized juices are safe if made at home
Wash produce and avoid buffets and unpasteurized foods

nutrition.rationale: Wash produce, cook foods safely, and avoid buffets/unpasteurized products; a blanket ban on all raw fruits/vegetables is not required.

nutrition.prompt: A client reports a metallic taste that is making meals unpleasant. Which suggestion may help?

options.text: Try metal utensils instead
Skip meals until it passes
Avoid protein foods for now
Try nonmetal utensils instead

nutrition.rationale: For metallic taste, nonmetal utensils may help, along with rinsing the mouth before meals. Skipping meals or protein compromises intake.

assessment.prompt: A client receiving doxorubicin followed by trastuzumab is being assessed. Which findings are most important?

options.text: Hearing, vision, and dental health history
Bone density and joint range of motion
Cardiac history, LVEF, edema, and dyspnea
Skin color, hair texture, and nail changes

assessment.rationale: For doxorubicin/HER2 therapy, assess cardiac history, ordered LVEF surveillance, edema, breathlessness, chest symptoms, and exercise tolerance. Both drugs can affect the heart; the other findings are not the key concern.

assessment.prompt: Before a client’s mastectomy with node surgery, which baseline should the nurse document?

options.text: Visual acuity in both eyes
Bowel sounds and abdomen
Hearing on whisper testing
Arm ROM, function, swelling

assessment.rationale: Before/after surgery, assess baseline arm ROM/function/swelling so later lymphedema or stiffness can be detected. Vision, hearing, and bowel sounds alone do not address this surgical risk.

diagnoses.prompt: A client on chemotherapy has an ANC of 600/microliter and an implanted port. Which nursing diagnosis is best supported?

options.text: Risk for aspiration
Excess fluid volume
Impaired swallowing
Risk for infection

diagnoses.rationale: Risk for infection relates to neutropenia, compromised skin, surgery, or vascular access. The others are not supported.

diagnoses.prompt: A neutropenic client has fever, hypotension, and confusion. How should the nurse treat this problem?

options.text: As a medical emergency for possible sepsis
As a learning need about fever teaching
As expected chemotherapy fatigue
As a routine problem for the next visit

diagnoses.rationale: Suspected sepsis is a medical emergency, not just an education need; it requires immediate escalation.

priorities.prompt: A client on chemotherapy arrives at triage with fever and suspected febrile neutropenia. Per ASCO/IDSA, when should the first antibiotic dose be given?

options.text: After a set period of fever observation
Within 1 hour of triage, without waiting for culture results
After the ANC result becomes available
Once the culture results have returned

priorities.rationale: For febrile neutropenia, give the prescribed initial empiric antibacterial dose within 1 hour of triage. Obtain indicated blood cultures promptly before antibiotics when this does not delay treatment; do not wait for culture results or delay urgent care for routine observation.

priorities.prompt: During a doxorubicin infusion, the client reports burning and swelling at the IV site. What is the nurse’s first action?

options.text: Flush the line briskly to clear the drug
Remove the catheter immediately and apply pressure
Slow the infusion rate and keep infusing
Stop the infusion and leave the access in place

priorities.rationale: For suspected vesicant extravasation, stop the infusion, leave access in place initially, do not flush, and activate the extravasation protocol for aspiration/antidote care. Flushing or continuing spreads the vesicant, and removing the catheter first prevents aspiration.

priorities.prompt: A client’s lab report shows an ANC in the severe neutropenia range. How should the nurse interpret this?

options.text: The neutrophil count is above normal
Infection risk is markedly increased
Infection risk is unchanged from normal
Infection risk is just slightly raised

priorities.rationale: Severe neutropenia (ANC <500/microliter) markedly raises infection risk, so fever or other infection signs need immediate action. It is a low—not high—neutrophil count, and the risk is neither normal nor slight.

plan.prompt: A client on trastuzumab had one normal LVEF and no fever this week. How should the nurse evaluate the emergency-detection goal?

options.text: Fever teaching has been completed
These alone don’t prove ongoing safety
Monitoring can stop at this point
Cardiac checks can now be spaced out

plan.rationale: “No fever” or “normal EF once” alone does not prove ongoing safety; trends and teach-back are evaluated.

plan.prompt: Which goal best reflects safe recovery after breast surgery?

options.text: Drains come out on one set day for each client
Pain allows sleep, ADLs, and shoulder exercise
Pain is gone by the first postoperative day
The arm is kept still until the wound heals

plan.rationale: The goal is pain acceptable for sleep/ADLs and prescribed shoulder movement, with wound/drain recovery per the plan. Zero pain, immobilizing the arm, or a fixed drain day are not appropriate goals.

interventions.prompt: The day after SLNB with blue dye, a client calls worried about blue-green urine. What is the nurse’s best response?

options.text: “The radiotracer may turn urine green.”
“This may be a kidney injury; go to the ED.”
“The dye may temporarily color the urine.”
“This may mean the cancer has spread.”

interventions.rationale: Blue dye—not the radiotracer—may temporarily discolor urine blue/green, commonly for a day or two; monitor for allergic reactions.

interventions.prompt: A client had axillary node surgery some time ago and needs a blood draw; the other arm has an infiltrated IV. Which statement guides the nurse?

options.text: Use the arm with the infiltrated IV site now
Evidence doesn’t support a strict lifelong ban
The at-risk arm is off-limits for procedures
Delay the blood draw until tomorrow instead

interventions.rationale: Evidence does not support a lifelong absolute ban on all blood draws or BP measurements in every at-risk arm after node surgery. Assess current swelling/lymphedema and the site, follow the individualized care plan and patient preferences, and use an unaffected site when feasible, especially with established lymphedema. Do not delay necessary care solely because of past node surgery.

interventions.prompt: A client is going home with a JP drain. What should the nurse have the client demonstrate?

options.text: Emptying, keeping suction, and recording output
Leaving the bulb fully expanded after emptying
Flushing the drain tubing daily with tap water
Removing the drain at home once output slows

interventions.rationale: Demonstrate emptying, maintaining suction, measuring/recording output, securement, and when to call; removal depends on the surgical plan.

education.prompt: A client is starting outpatient chemotherapy. What should she keep at home?

options.text: Acetaminophen to bring fevers down at home
A supply of antibiotics to start on her own
A working thermometer and oncology phone numbers
A blood pressure cuff for daily home readings

education.rationale: Keep a working thermometer and written oncology day/after-hours numbers; masking fever with antipyretics delays care.

education.prompt: A breast cancer survivor says, “I’ll just get a mammogram every 2 years like everyone else.” What should the nurse teach?

options.text: Post-treatment follow-up differs from screening
She can stop breast imaging once treatment ends
Follow-up ends as soon as treatment is finished
Average-risk screening is enough for her from now

education.rationale: Routine screening schedules for average-risk people do not substitute for post-treatment follow-up; follow the oncology surveillance plan.

evaluation.prompt: A client on trastuzumab feels well and asks to skip her LVEF scan. How should the nurse respond?

options.text: She may skip it if she has no breathlessness
LVEF checks are optional during this therapy
Check LVEF once treatment has ended instead
Having no symptoms doesn’t replace the check

evaluation.rationale: Absence of symptoms alone does not replace scheduled LVEF monitoring, as cardiac dysfunction may be silent. LVEF checks are a required part of HER2 therapy monitoring.

evaluation.prompt: Which finding best indicates recovery after breast surgery is on track?

options.text: Shoulder/arm function improves with activity
The arm has been kept still since the surgery
Drain output has not been measured or recorded
New arm swelling is present but not assessed

evaluation.rationale: Recovery is evaluated by manageable pain and shoulder/arm function improving with prescribed activity; new swelling must be assessed.
